entities.summary:
The Odyssey, attributed to the ancient Greek poet Homer, is a foundational epic of Western literature, composed around the 8th century BCE, during the height of the Archaic period in Greece. Its narrative, set against the backdrop of the Mediterranean world, chronicles the adventurous return of Odysseus, King of Ithaca, from the Trojan War, which itself is a seminal event in Greek mythology and history. This epic not only provides insight into ancient Greek values such as heroism, loyalty, and the struggle against fate but also serves as a critical cultural artifact that has shaped the literary canon and influenced countless works throughout the ages.

The events of The Odyssey unfold over ten years after the conclusion of the Trojan War, detailing Odysseus's encounters with mythical creatures and divine beings, such as the Cyclops Polyphemus and the sorceress Circe. The poem's structure is non-linear, employing flashbacks and multiple perspectives, which was innovative for its time. Key locations in Odysseus's journey, such as the island of Ithaca and the land of the Phaeacians, highlight the geographical imagination of ancient Greeks and their understanding of the world. The text emphasizes themes of perseverance, identity, and the importance of cleverness, embodied in Odysseus's character, who embodies the archetype of the cunning hero.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Odyssey (Ancient Greek: Ὀδύσσεια, Odysseia) is an ancient Greek epic poem attributed to Homer, composed in the 8th century BCE and regarded as one of the foundational texts of Western literature and world literary culture. The poem narrates in 24 books (approximately 12,110 lines of dactylic hexameter) the ten-year homeward journey of the hero Odysseus (Ulysses in Latin tradition) from Troy to his kingdom of Ithaca after the Trojan War — a journey complicated by divine wrath (the sea-god Poseidon), supernatural obstacles (the Cyclops Polyphemus, the witch Circe, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis), the temptations of immortality (the nymph Calypso), and the suitors who have invaded his household and court his wife Penelope in his absence.

The Odyssey is the paradigmatic text of the literary journey — the archetype from which all subsequent quest narratives, voyage tales, and homecoming stories derive their fundamental structure. The Homeric concept of nostos (νόστος, homecoming) gave English the word 'nostalgia' (coined in 1688 by Swiss physician Johannes Hofer from nóstos and álgos, 'pain'), and Odysseus's journey has been read as the prototype for the human condition of exile, longing, and return. The poem's episodic structure — each island a different trial, each encounter a different temptation or ordeal — established the episodic quest narrative as a fundamental literary form.

The Odyssey's influence on Western literature is incalculable — James Joyce's Ulysses (1922) uses the Odyssey as its structural framework, mapping Homer's episodes onto a single day in Dublin; Tennyson's Ulysses (1833) reimagines Odysseus in old age; Dante's Inferno (Canto 26) gives Odysseus a tragic final voyage beyond the pillars of Hercules; and the figure of the cunning, resourceful wanderer seeking home — the 'man of many devices' (polytropos) — is one of the most pervasive archetypes in world narrative.
